extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral and political philosophy (general educated readership)
extracted.subtask_description: A close analysis of what determines human will and choice: the primacy of present uneasiness/pain in motivating action, the role of desire and judgment, and the relation of suspension-of-desire to liberty. Explains why absent goods (even infinitely greater ones) often fail to determine action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of Uneasiness is the first Step to Happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: While we all aim at happiness, the present uneasiness or pain we feel operates on the will and determines choice because as long as we are uneasy we cannot apprehend ourselves happy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pain and uneasiness are felt to be inconsistent with happiness and spoil present pleasures; therefore the next action will naturally be aimed at removing present uneasiness as the first necessary step toward happiness. Example: a person in pain will act to relieve it even when greater future goods are known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uneasiness alone is present (absent goods do not operate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Absent goods, though contemplated, are not present goods and cannot counterbalance removal of present uneasiness until they raise desire and become present in the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An idea of an absent good is mere speculative representation and does not move the will until it produces desire; therefore contemplation of remote goods (e.g., heaven) often fails to prompt action. The only way to make absent good operative is to bring it nearer through repeated consideration that raises desire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absent greater goods often fail to determine the will
rubrics_metrics.description: If the will were determined by contemplated greater goods, once the infinite good (e.g., heavenly joy) is proposed it would always hold the will; but in experience even the greatest absent good is often neglected in favor of present uneasiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This claims an empirical constraint on motivational theories: mere recognition of a greater good does not guarantee sustained motivation — probability and presentness matter. Anti-pattern: assuming 'rightness' of an end is sufficient to produce action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Any great present Uneasiness keeps the will fixed
rubrics_metrics.description: A vehement present uneasiness (e.g., bodily pain, passionate love, desire for revenge) will keep the will intent and uninterruptedly employed on actions to remove it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong immediate passions monopolize thought and action; they prevent the will from shifting toward absent goods until they subside. Example: intense pain or passionate fury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desire accompanies all Uneasiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The will seldom orders voluntary action without some desire; wherever there is uneasiness there is desire, and desire typically accompanies passions (aversion, fear, anger, envy, shame).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This explains frequent conflation of will and desire; even pleasures include the desire to continue and the fear of losing them. Implication: motivational analysis should treat desire as the proximate companion of uneasiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: The most pressing Uneasiness naturally determines the Will
rubrics_metrics.description: When beset by many uneasinesses, ordinarily the most pressing one judged capable of being removed determines the next action of the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The will aims at actions judged attainable; very great uneasiness judged incurable may not move the will. Practical rule: in decision sequences, priority goes to the strongest solvable discomfort.

rubrics_metrics.name: All desire Happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness (and avoidance of misery) is the ultimate object that moves desire; what is judged to contribute to one's happiness is desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good and evil are relative in degrees and comparison; goods are desired insofar as they are judged necessary parts of an individual's happiness. Use this when explaining why different people pursue different ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only that part of good taken as part of one's happiness is desired
rubrics_metrics.description: A person does not desire all acknowledged goods — only the portion considered necessary to his or her own happiness; other goods can be acknowledged without desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: one person values sensual pleasures, another knowledge; each may see the other's good as good but not desired. Practical implication: motivating someone requires making the good appear a necessary part of their personal happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why the greatest visible good is not always desired
rubrics_metrics.description: Because absent goods do not necessarily form part of present happiness, and because present pains and ordinary wants occupy life, people often content themselves with moderate present goods rather than pursuing a greater absent good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains commonplace indifference to distant or abstract goods despite recognizing their magnitude. Anti-pattern: expecting constant pursuit of the objectively greatest good regardless of present circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present necessities and habitual desires crowd out consideration of remote goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary necessities (hunger, thirst, sleep), acquired habits and fashions create continual uneasinesses that leave little vacancy for attraction to remoter absent goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of a constant succession of solicitations, present uneasinesses justify prioritization; absent goods can only compete after due repeated contemplation has raised desire. Recommendation: create repeated, salient contemplation to make absent goods compete successfully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due Consideration raises Desire
rubrics_metrics.description: By due consideration and examination, it is possible to raise desires proportionally to the value of an absent good, making it operative on the will.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical strategy: careful reflection and repeated attention can convert an acknowledged absent good into a present desire that can determine will and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to suspend desire enables examination (source of liberty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humans have the power to suspend immediate satisfaction of desires, allowing time to examine objects of desire and judge their good or evil; this suspension is the hinge of liberty (often called free will).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liberty consists in being able to delay action until due consideration; withholding premature engagement prevents many errors. Example: resisting an immediate impulse to consider long-term consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Being determined by one's judgment is not a restraint on liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Acting according to the last result of a fair examination (one's own judgment) is not a diminution of freedom; indeed, it is the expression of proper liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes between arbitrary indifference and responsible determination; true liberty includes both the ability to suspend and the capacity to be determined by informed judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfectly happy beings are more steadily determined by good but not less free
rubrics_metrics.description: Superior beings who enjoy perfect happiness are more steadily determined in choosing what is good, yet that determination does not make them less free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative theological point: freedom is compatible with being necessarily inclined toward the best; being determined by the best is a perfection, not a loss of liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspense and deliberation are required by pursuit of true happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity of pursuing true happiness obliges agents to suspend particular desires and scrutinize whether satisfying a given desire is consistent with the main goal of true happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral recommendation: cultivate the habit of deferring immediate satisfaction when the weight of the matter requires examination; doing so fulfills duty and preserves liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power to Suspend (restated as hinge of liberty)
rubrics_metrics.description: The specific faculty to suspend prosecution of a desire until one has informed oneself about its relation to the main end is the central feature of liberty in finite intellectual beings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When this power is exercised properly, agents do their duty by examining good and evil to the degree required by the matter's importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government of passions improves liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: Restraint and moderation of passions so the understanding may examine and judge unbiassedly is the right improvement of liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If violent passions overwhelm deliberation (e.g., rack pain, impetuous love, anger), then agents are not blameworthy beyond their power; otherwise cultivating self-control is a moral duty to preserve liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety of pursuits explained by differing conceptions of happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Different people pursue different courses (study, luxury, hunting) because they place happiness in different things; the variety does not prove they do not aim at their own good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: tastes differ as palates differ; ethical debates about the single 'summum bonum' miss that individuals locate happiness in different items. Practical implication: normative claims must account for differing value-frames.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes why people choose what makes them miserable
rubrics_metrics.description: People sometimes prefer worse to better due to various uneasinesses that determine the will: (1) bodily pain (necessity), (2) wrong desires arising from wrong judgments about absent good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: extreme poverty or bodily suffering can force choices contrary to long-term happiness; mistaken judgments about what is necessary to happiness mislead desires. Prescriptive: address causal sources (relieve necessity, correct judgments) to change choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgment about present good or evil is reliable
rubrics_metrics.description: When only present states matter, a person rarely chooses wrongly because present pleasure/pain is as it appears — the apparent and real good coincide for present enjoyment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mistakes arise when actions have remote consequences; immediate choices based solely on present sensation are usually accurate. Use this to separate errors of foresight from errors of perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrong judgments concern future goods and evils
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors in choice stem mainly from mistaken opinions about future benefits or harms, since voluntary actions often have consequences after they are performed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy implication: improving foresight and judgment about consequences will reduce choices that favor immediate satisfaction but produce longer-term misery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrong judgment about what makes a necessary part of happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: People often think they can be happy without certain great absent goods; this belief prevents desire and leaves the will free to pursue nearer satisfactions, thereby explaining neglect of greater absent goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To motivate pursuit of greater goods, one must make them appear necessary parts of one's present conception of happiness (through reflection, education, or habit formation).
